Junkanoo. A vibrant Bahamian street parade that celebrates the New Year, held on Boxing Day and New Year's Day, featuring elaborate costumes, floats, horns, drums, and dancing. The festival is rooted in African and Caribbean traditions and reflects the cultural heritage of enslaved peoples who were historically given a few days off around Christmas and New Year.

The January parade is the larger and more famous celebration. The name's origin is debated, possibly derived from John Canoe, an African tribal chief, or from French gens inconnus, meaning unknown people, which reflects the tradition of partygoers wearing masks. Participants construct elaborate papier-mache floats and costumes featuring brilliant colors, geometric patterns, and imaginative designs crafted over months of planning.

The distinctive instruments include cowbells, whistles, drums, conch shells, and metal horns creating a cacophonous celebratory sound throughout Nassau and other Bahamian islands. Groups compete for prizes, with each parade group called a rush, comprising dozens or hundreds of costumed dancers and musicians dancing behind their float. Steel bands, gospel choirs, and traditional rake-and-scrape music blend with modern Caribbean sounds.
